title: Learning Pareto Stationary Fronts via Single-Pass Backpropagation
claim: A model splits into a representation network and a preference-conditioned alignment network, so one forward pass yields many trade-offs.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right; dotted lines zoom block diagram into ResNet detail
description: Two stacked panels. Panel (a) is a horizontal flow of rounded boxes: Input x, Representation Learning Network f_θ, Preference Alignment Network g_φ, Output ŷ(x;r) and Loss. Gray boxes are the networks and blue-gray boxes are the data and loss. The intermediate feature z = f_θ(x) passes between the two networks, and a preference vector r ~ Dir(α) enters the alignment network from below. Dotted lines connect the two networks to panel (b), which expands them on a ResNet-34. It shows an input image, then stacked orange feature-map icons for Conv1 and Res layers 1–3 with their dimensions. A FiLM layer box then maps r through a green Linear layer to scale γ and shift β, with the equation z' = γ⊙z + β. The result feeds Res layer 4 and FC. The eye goes first to the top row of boxes, then down to the zoomed detail.
caption: Overview of MOSEL. (a) It partitions the neural network into a representation learning network, steering z toward Pareto optimal solutions, and a preference alignment network conditioning on r ∼Dir(α) to cover diverse trade-offs. (b) Illustration on ResNet-34 [20]: z is extracted at the network split point and modulated via a FiLM layer [50], which maps r to a scaling and shift factor per feature channel, steering the final predictions ˆy(x; r) toward the desired objective trade-off.
abstract: We propose MOSEL (Multi-Objective Stackelberg Efficient Learning), a framework for a posteriori multi-objective optimization (MOO) in deep neural networks that recovers a full front of Pareto stationary solutions at the computational cost of standard single-objective training. MOSEL reformulates the problem as a bilevel optimization problem that leverages network modularity to decouple representation learning from objective-preference alignment. Casting the bilevel optimization problem as a Stackelberg game enables solving the original a posteriori MOO problem in a single forward-backward pass. As a result, MOSEL matches the time and memory efficiency of standard single-objective training while enabling scalable Pareto stationary front learning. Empirically, MOSEL uncovers diverse and optimal Pareto frontiers in strongly conflicting settings (e.g., fairness-accuracy). Remarkably, even in weakly conflicting regimes such as multi-task learning, it consistently converges to solutions closer to the utopia point, outperforming both standard single-objective training and specialized multi-task learning methods. These results highlight the broader potential of a posteriori MOO learning as a pathway to efficiently learn more diverse and robust representations, ultimately improving generalization.
